meta.title: Who really said "A Verbal Contract Isn't Worth the Paper It's Written On"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Samuel Goldwyn. The gag was in print by 1890, credited to Sir Bryan O'Loghlen; a 1937 biography pinned it on Goldwyn, who later denied it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Verbal Contract Isn't Worth the Paper It's Written On'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to 1890 and Sir Bryan O'Loghlen. The line reached Goldwyn through a 1937 biography — and he denied it.

answer.label: Not Samuel Goldwyn — credited to Sir Bryan O'Loghlen
answer.authorDates: 1828–1905 · Irish-born barrister & 13th Premier of Victoria, Australia
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the gag to The Irish Law Times and Solicitors’ Journal of 14 June 1890, which reported that Sir Bryan O’Loghlen, M.P. — in the colony of Victoria — “gravely told the Supreme Court that ‘a verbal agreement is not worth the paper it’s written on.’” QI credits O’Loghlen while noting the same joke was circulating anonymously at the time, and hypothesises that Goldwyn never used the line at all: it only became his when Alva Johnston’s The Great Goldwyn (1937) ↗ printed it as a genuine Goldwynism.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Irish Law Times and Solicitors’ Journal, 14 June 1890, p. 320
Alva Johnston, The Great Goldwyn (Random House, 1937), p. 16
Reported denying the Goldwynisms — Dallas Morning News, 12 February 1956

source.excerpt: Sam said, “Gentlemen, include me out.” It would be impossible to make a more pointed remark than Goldwyn’s, “A verbal contract isn’t worth the paper it’s written on.”
trail: 14 June 1890 — The Irish Law Times and Solicitors’ Journal, p. 320, reports that “Sir Bryan O’Loghlen, M.P., who has a national right to indulge in this sort of thing, gravely told the Supreme Court that ‘a verbal agreement is not worth the paper it’s written on.’” This is the earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ documents.

1890–1905 — the joke spreads without an author. A September 1890 Rocky Mountain News item gives it to a stock Irish character; an 1894 collection credits “an Australian lawyer”; an 1897 review ties it to Sir Boyle Roche. The Cleveland Leader of 25 April 1905 prints the exact modern wording — “a verbal contract isn’t worth the paper it’s written on!” — in an anonymous dialogue, per QI ↗.
12 December 1926 — comedian Ed Wynn runs it in his syndicated column in the Seattle Daily Times. QI ↗ notes he was using a jest already in circulation, not coining one.

1937 — Alva Johnston’s The Great Goldwyn puts it in Goldwyn’s mouth on page 16 ↗ — the first attribution to him. By 12 February 1956 a Dallas Morning News column was reporting that Goldwyn “denies vehemently” the sayings pinned on him, listing a close variant of this one among them.
source.excerptNote: In the paragraph immediately before this one, on the same page, Johnston concedes that “Goldwyn’s publicity department formerly collected and invented Goldwyn gags and circulated them,” and that “today it takes an expert to pick the genuine Goldwyn lines from the spurious.” He then files this line among the genuine ones — a line that had been in print since 1890.

source.rightsNote: The sentence itself is public domain in the United States: it is documented in print in The Irish Law Times and Solicitors’ Journal in June 1890 and in this exact wording in the Cleveland Leader of April 1905 — both decades before the 1931 US copyright threshold, and both by authors long dead. Note that the excerpt shown above is a short quotation from a separate and much later work, Alva Johnston’s The Great Goldwyn (Random House, 1937), reproduced here for commentary on how the misattribution began.

author.name: Sir Bryan O’Loghlen
author.kicker: The man Quote Investigator actually credits
author.heading: The Irish barrister who out-Goldwyned Goldwyn
author.bio: Sir Bryan O’Loghlen, 3rd Baronet, was admitted to the Irish Bar in 1856, emigrated to Australia and served as a Crown Prosecutor in Victoria from 1863, then as the colony’s Attorney-General and, from 1881 to 1883, as its 13th Premier. He is the figure The Irish Law Times named in 1890 as the man who told the Supreme Court that a verbal agreement was not worth the paper it was written on — a remark the journal treated as a splendid specimen of the Irish bull. Quote Investigator calls it reasonable to credit him, while cautioning that the same joke was already being told by anonymous characters in newspaper gags, so the ascription may itself have been manufactured.

misattribution.heading: Who has been credited — and why it stuck to Goldwyn
misattribution.intro: Search the line today and almost every quotation site returns Samuel Goldwyn. The print record runs the other way: by the time Goldwyn was ever associated with it, the joke had been circulating for nearly five decades under several different names.

items.why: First printed as his in Alva Johnston’s The Great Goldwyn (1937), p. 16 — decades after the joke entered print. Quote Investigator ↗ states plainly that it “hypothesizes that Goldwyn never employed this phrase,” and Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Misattributed.

The comedian ran “A verbal contract, in my opinion, is not worth the paper it is written on” in his syndicated column in the Seattle Daily Times of 12 December 1926. QI ↗ notes he “used the jest when it was already in circulation.”

An 1897 item in The Contemporary Review connected the saying to Roche, per QI ↗. Roche is the figure most often called the “father” of the Irish bull ↗, which makes him a natural magnet for unattached examples of the form — the same role Goldwyn would later play.

items.who: Joseph M. Schenck, or Joseph L. Mankiewicz
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ calls the famous line “a misreporting of an actual quote praising the trustworthiness of a colleague: ‘His verbal contract is worth more than the paper it’s written on’,” naming Schenck (Boller & George, They Never Said It, 1990, p. 42) or Mankiewicz (Easton, The Search for Sam Goldwyn, 1976). This could explain the transmission, but not the origin: the joke predates Goldwyn’s career.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is documented in print from 14 June 1890 and in its exact modern wording by 25 April 1905, long before anyone attached it to Samuel Goldwyn — and in 1956 Goldwyn was reported denying the Goldwynisms hung on him. See the full chronology at Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why a nonsense sentence outlived the man it was pinned on
lead: The line is a perfect Irish bull ↗ — a statement that collapses under its own logic while somehow still making its point. A verbal contract has no paper; that is the whole idea of it. The joke works because the speaker seems not to notice, and because the sentiment underneath (get it in writing) is sound legal advice. Nineteenth-century law reporters loved that combination, which is exactly why The Irish Law Times printed it in 1890 as a specimen of the form rather than as a piece of wisdom.

Samuel Goldwyn’s role came later, and it was structural rather than personal. By the 1930s he had become what Quote Investigator calls “a magnet for malapropisms” — an address that unattached jokes were simply delivered to. Alva Johnston, writing the first book-length portrait of him in 1937, described the mechanism on the very page where he then repeated this line as authentic: Goldwyn’s publicity department had collected and invented gags and put them into circulation, until “it takes an expert to pick the genuine Goldwyn lines from the spurious.” Johnston diagnosed the disease and caught it in the same breath.
context.detailsSummary: The rival theory: an inverted compliment
detailsBody: Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ offers a different explanation of how the sentence reached Goldwyn: that it is a garbling of a real compliment he paid a colleague — “His verbal contract is worth more than the paper it’s written on” — the colleague being identified as Joseph M. Schenck in Paul F. Boller and John George’s They Never Said It (1990), p. 42, or as Joseph L. Mankiewicz in Carol Easton’s The Search for Sam Goldwyn (1976).

That story may well explain why the line stuck to Goldwyn so firmly. It cannot explain where the line came from, because the joke was in print in 1890 and in its exact modern wording in 1905, well before Goldwyn was a producer. Treat it as a plausible account of the transmission, not of the origin.
context.pull: A verbal contract has no paper. That is the joke — and it was being told in courtrooms decades before Hollywood existed.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest documented instance is The Irish Law Times and Solicitors' Journal, 14 June 1890, p. 320, crediting Sir Bryan O'Loghlen with 'a verbal agreement is not worth the paper it's written on'; the Cleveland Leader of 25 April 1905 carries the exact modern wording; Ed Wynn ran it in the Seattle Daily Times on 12 December 1926; Alva Johnston's The Great Goldwyn (1937), p. 16 first attributed it to Goldwyn; a Dallas Morning News column of 12 February 1956 reported Goldwyn denying the Goldwynisms; and QI concludes 'QI hypothesizes that Goldwyn never employed this phrase.'

The Great Goldwyn by Alva Johnston (Random House, 1937) prints on page 16: 'Sam said, "Gentlemen, include me out." It would be impossible to make a more pointed remark than Goldwyn's, "A verbal contract isn't worth the paper it's written on."' — and in the immediately preceding paragraph on the same page states that 'Goldwyn's publicity department formerly collected and invented Goldwyn gags and circulated them' and 'Today it takes an expert to pick the genuine Goldwyn lines from the spurious.'

Wikiquote lists 'A verbal contract isn't worth the paper it's written on' under its Misattributed section for Samuel Goldwyn, describing it as 'A misreporting of an actual quote praising the trustworthiness of a colleague: "His verbal contract is worth more than the paper it's written on"', with the colleague identified as Joseph M. Schenk in Boller & George, They Never Said It (1990), p. 42, or Joseph L. Mankiewicz in Carol Easton, The Search for Sam Goldwyn (1976).

Sir Bryan O'Loghlen, 3rd Baronet (27 June 1828 – 31 October 1905) was an Irish-born Australian colonial politician, the 13th Premier of Victoria (1881–1883), admitted to the Irish Bar in 1856, Crown Prosecutor in Victoria from 1863 and Attorney-General of Victoria from 1878.

Wikipedia states that 'Goldwynisms were the inventions of humorists and newspaper editors' and that 'Many famous "Goldwynisms" predate Goldwyn's career as circulated witticism'; it gives his birth name as Szmuel Gelbfisz and his death date as 31 January 1974.

Wikipedia defines an Irish bull as 'a ludicrous, incongruent or logically absurd statement, generally unrecognized as such by its author' and states that 'The "father" of the Irish bull is often said to be Sir Boyle Roche'. (It does not itself list the verbal-contract example.)
The Irish Law Times (originally the Irish Law Times and Solicitors' Journal) is an Irish professional law journal founded in 1865.
